intro.es: A town celebrates the success of a reusable cup scheme. Its figures become less certain when a volunteer asks what lies beyond the return counter.

mission.es: Trace how changing the boundary of a measurement changes the meaning of an environmental success.
mission.en: Trace how changing the boundary of a measurement changes the meaning of an environmental success.

content.targetText:
The town's returnable cup scheme began with an admirably modest ambition: reduce the paper cups left around the market after Saturday lunch. A small deposit brought the new cups back to a counter beside the fountain, and the organisers counted each return with a satisfying click. At the end of the first summer, they announced that the scheme had prevented thousands of disposable cups from entering the bins. The number appeared on posters, then on the mayor's speech, and finally on a mural beside the station. I helped paint that mural. At the time I thought the neat row of cups we drew was a fair symbol of what we had done. The square was cleaner; vendors spent less on rubbish bags; children had learned to carry their empty cups back. None of those gains was imaginary. The mural became less comfortable to look at only after someone asked where the returned cups went next.

Every evening a driver took them to a washing facility beyond the town. Its machines were efficient, according to the contractor, but efficiency described the water and energy used per wash, not the distance of a journey made for a half-full van. The cups themselves were durable when treated as the supplier intended. At the market, however, the handles met stone steps, the lids were lost, and a cup with a hairline crack could no longer be served. The contractor's report classified such cups as recycled. We later learned that this meant they were delivered to a broker; the report did not follow what the broker managed to sell. To call the original count false would be too easy. Each click at the fountain marked a cup that really had returned. What the count could not show was whether returning had made that cup more useful than the resources required to receive, wash and move it. The scheme had measured a visible substitution and allowed that measure to stand for the entire journey.

At a public meeting, Lila, who ran the smallest coffee stall, asked whether the council had considered the cups' effect on her staff. People returned them at closing time, when her two assistants were already cleaning the counter. A larger cafe had space to stack the cups until morning; Lila kept a crate in the narrow passage to her sink. The scheme had not created this difference in floor space, but its rules treated all vendors as if they operated from interchangeable rooms. The mayor replied that adjustments could be made once the environmental benefit was established. His sequence sounded prudent: prove a benefit, then distribute its costs more fairly. Yet Lila's cramped passage was part of the cost of obtaining the benefit, not an unrelated grievance to be considered afterward. Her question altered the unit of account. We were no longer weighing a cup against a paper cup, but an arrangement of work against another arrangement of work.

The council commissioned a broader study. I expected it to settle the argument, and was initially disappointed when it produced three conclusions rather than one. If a cup was used often and the washing van was full, the returnable scheme performed well by the study's chosen environmental measures. If a cup broke early or travelled in an almost empty van, the advantage narrowed and sometimes reversed. The third conclusion was the least photogenic: a better loading schedule could matter more than persuading another hundred customers to pay a deposit. Several councillors called these findings inconclusive. They were conditional, which is different. A condition can tell a manager what to change; a single triumphant total cannot. But the new study also had a boundary. It priced fuel and water with more care than it represented the inconvenience of a crowded passage or the time a visitor spent finding a return counter. To include everything would have made the study unfinishable. To include only what was easy to count would have made it deceptively complete.

We repainted the mural the following spring. The neat row of cups stayed, but the number was replaced with a small diagram showing a loop from stall to counter to washer and back. It had no space for Lila's passage, the broker's warehouse or the question of who carried a cup home when the counter had closed. A mural is a poor substitute for an audit; perhaps it need not be one. I still use a returnable cup at the market, and I still return it. I have become wary, though, of describing that gesture as a completed act of environmental repair. It is a contribution to a system whose results depend on maintenance, transport and the work assigned to people with unequal room to absorb it. The scheme improved when the town admitted that its celebrated number was a partial account. Some residents took the admission as a retreat. For me it made the claim more credible: a success willing to specify its conditions is more useful than one that demands deference to its own headline.
